cards.title: Run a 16-question validation pass before sourcing any physical product
cards.summary: A structured 16-point checklist that screens a product idea across market, competition, economics, logistics and retention before you spend on inventory.
cards.use_when: You have a physical product idea and want an objective go/no-go screen before committing time, sourcing spend or manufacturing.
steps: Split the checklist into two blocks: market-level questions (demand size, competitor landscape, trend direction, local availability, target customer) and product-level questions (selling price, markup, SKU count, subscription fit, size/weight, durability, seasonality, pain vs passion, consumability, perishability, restrictions).
Work market questions first: they can kill an idea before you spend effort on unit economics.
Score each question as pass, caution or red flag rather than a binary yes/no. The source stresses that not every box will be checked.

At the end, write an explicit list of highlights and concerns for the idea. In the source's coconut hair mask example, highlights were low startup cost, strong search demand, upward trend and rankable keywords; concerns were the low price point and fragmented competition.
Only proceed when the concerns look fixable through branding, differentiation or positioning rather than through hoping the numbers change.
caveats: This is a baseline screening framework, not a guarantee of demand. The source explicitly says search volume and social mentions are a 'vote of confidence' in interest, not proof of buyers.
Validator work does not replace supplier negotiation, sourcing or storefront build, which sit in other workflows.

cards.title: Size demand with Keyword Planner search volume plus social mention volume
cards.summary: Use free search-volume and social-listening tools to estimate whether enough people are actively looking for the product before investing.
cards.use_when: You need a first quantitative read on demand for a product concept and have not yet chosen suppliers.
steps: Open Google Keyword Planner (free) and query the core keywords and close variants that describe your product idea, e.g. 'coconut oil hair mask'.
Record the combined monthly search volume. In the source example, related terms returned roughly 73,000 searches per month.
Use a social listening tool such as BuzzSumo to count how many people mention the main keywords per day. The example found around 150 tweets per day.
Read the two numbers together as a demand signal, not a forecast: high search volume plus steady social chatter indicates live interest.
Cross-check the keyword direction in Google Trends (see the trend-direction card) because a large but shrinking search base can still be a bad bet.
caveats: Keyword Planner volume is an estimate and can be inflated by broad-match terms; the source treats it as directional.
Social mentions include people discussing, not buying. High chatter with no commercial intent language is weaker evidence.

cards.title: Classify the market direction: growing, flat, fad or declining
cards.summary: Use Google Trends and trend research to separate a durable upward category from a passing fad or a market you have already missed.
cards.use_when: Demand volume looks acceptable and you need to judge whether the category will still exist in two to three years.
steps: Plot the main and adjacent keywords in Google Trends over the longest available window and look at the trajectory, not a single month.
Label the pattern: consistently rising, flat, spiking and collapsing (fad), or declining.

Research why the trend is moving. In the source example, coconut oil interest had grown over several years, but the presenter notes that the beauty industry rotates new 'breakthrough' ingredients, so an ingredient trend can eventually die.
Use trend-hunting resources or your own category intuition when the data is ambiguous; the source notes many entrepreneurs rely on gut instinct for trend timing.
Treat a rising trend as a green light for entry but plan for it to flatten, and avoid building the whole business around a single fashionable ingredient or format.
caveats: The source's own case study shows a rising trend that may still decline, so treat trend direction as a risk factor rather than an anchor.
Trend tools are external services whose interfaces and output change; verify current functionality before relying on them.

cards.title: Map competitors, including free and DIY substitutes
cards.summary: Research the competitive landscape in your target markets, treating grocery-store alternatives and homemade substitutes as real competitors.
cards.use_when: You are validating a product category and want to know whether there is room for a new entrant.
steps: Search Google in each country you intend to sell in, using the language customers would use, not your internal product name.

List every credible substitute, not just branded products. In the source example three competitive areas emerged: pure coconut oil sold in grocery stores, DIY recipes, and commercial products from large businesses.

Note whether the market is dominated by a recognizable leader or is fragmented among many manufacturers and retailers. The source treats a fragmented market with no true market leaders as a possible opportunity signal.
Check offline availability directly. If the product is easy to buy at a local store, online viability drops because there is one less reason to order online; scarcity offline is a positive sign.
Fold the result into your overall concern list rather than declaring victory: fragmentation can mean opportunity or simply that nobody has made the category work online.
caveats: Fragmentation is ambiguous: the source calls it a possible opportunity, not proof of a viable gap.
A market with major incumbents is harder to read; the source suggests using traffic and demographic estimates on incumbent sites to learn about the buyer.

cards.title: Profile target customers before committing to a product
cards.summary: Estimate who the buyers are, where they live and whether they buy online, so you do not discover unshippable or unreachable demand too late.
cards.use_when: You need to confirm the product's audience is reachable and in a country you can ship to and advertise in.
steps: If major competitors have websites, use audience-estimation tools to read the demographics of their traffic as a proxy for the category's buyers.
If the market is too fragmented for that, sample social platforms directly: read posts and profiles that use your keywords and infer gender and age range.
In the source example, the people tweeting about coconut hair masks were mostly female, with an inferred average age of 18 to 35.
Use Google Trends region data to see which countries dominate the interest. The example showed the US and Canada.
Check that the demographic is comfortable buying online and that shipping to the identified countries is feasible; the source treats the ability to reach the audience easily as a strong positive.
Capture this profile now, because it feeds creative, channel choice and pricing later.
caveats: Profile-image and tweet-based demographic inference is a rough estimate. The source presents it as a feel for the audience when no incumbent data exists.
Trend region data shows where search happens, not where people are willing to pay international shipping.

cards.title: Target the $50–$150 retail price band for paid-acquisition economics
cards.summary: A commonly cited sweet spot where a product carries enough margin to fund paid ads but is not so expensive that buyers expect premium service.
cards.use_when: You are choosing between product concepts or setting an initial retail price for a product you intend to acquire customers for with paid ads.
steps: Price-check comparable products from at least a couple of dozen brands to establish the category's realistic band. In the source example about two dozen comparable hair masks implied roughly $9–$20 for 120ml.
Compare that band against the widely cited $50–$150 sweet spot used by many ecommerce operators.
Reason about both ends: below the band, per-unit profit is too thin to absorb paid advertising; above it, customers hesitate online and expect premium service such as phone support.
If your product's realistic price sits below the band, treat it as a red flag for a paid-traffic-first business rather than an automatic reject, as the source does with the hair mask example.
Flag low-price products as candidates for organic traffic, bundles, larger sizes or a higher-value-positioned formulation instead of a straight paid-ads launch.
caveats: The $50–$150 range is described in the source as generally accepted by many top ecommerce entrepreneurs, not a proven law; it may not apply to categories with strong repeat purchase or cheap organic acquisition.
The source's own case study sat at $9–$20 and was flagged as a margin risk, showing low price is a caution rather than a disqualifier.

cards.title: Model markup at low and high price points, including future bulk costing
cards.summary: Estimate cost per unit and profit per unit across the plausible price range so a single bad price assumption does not sink the business.
cards.use_when: You have a rough price band and a first cost estimate and need to see whether the product can carry your expenses.
steps: Estimate all-in cost of goods for an initial small run: ingredients or components, packaging, and any assembly. In the source example producing 100 units cost about $583, i.e. roughly $5.83 per unit.
Compute markup at the bottom and the top of your realistic price band, not just the middle. At $9 the source's example markup was a concern; at $20 it was healthy.
List what markup must cover: operating expenses, marketing and profit.
Model how cost changes as order volume grows, since bulk pricing lowers unit cost and increases the leftover margin as you scale.
If markup only works at the top of the band, verify that buyers will actually pay the top price before sourcing.
caveats: The source's $583 per 100 units is a case-study figure, not a benchmark for any other product.
Early cost estimates often omit inbound freight, duties, payment fees and returns; treat this as a first-pass screen.

cards.title: Launch with exactly one SKU and treat extra variants as complexity debt
cards.summary: Minimize SKUs at launch because each variant adds inventory capital, storage cost and shipping-error risk.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how many sizes, colors or formulations to launch with.
steps: Default the launch to a single SKU. The source calls a one-SKU product a bonus.
Treat each additional SKU as three costs: more inventory capital tied up, more storage cost, and a higher chance of picking and shipping the wrong item.

Use the single SKU as the starting wedge, then expand into a line only after the core product proves out. The source notes that a one-SKU concept can later extend into a full line, which opens opportunities down the road.
If the category demands variants (e.g. sizes), pick the single best-selling configuration first and let demand data justify the next one.
caveats: A single SKU limits the baskets you can build from the start; the source presents it as a risk-minimization trade-off, not a permanent rule.
Some categories cannot compete credibly without shade or size ranges.

cards.title: Judge subscription fit by real consumption rate, not category type
cards.summary: Subscriptions are desirable but only work when the customer genuinely repurchases often enough to justify the cadence.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating whether a product can support recurring revenue and lower blended acquisition cost.
steps: Check the product's fundamental nature first: consumable and disposable products such as supplements, cosmetics, foods and cleaning products create natural repeat purchase.

Then estimate real consumption. In the source example the hair mask was consumable, but a customer would likely use only a couple per year, so any subscription plan would have to reflect that slow cadence.
Set the replenishment interval from observed usage rather than an aggressive default; a mismatched cadence produces churn and refunds.
Note that subscription capability is desirable but not required: the source explicitly says subscriptions are not necessary to build a successful online business.
If repeat purchase is slow, model retention value from consumable resale and bundles rather than a monthly plan.
caveats: Slow-consumption products still help retention but cannot support high-frequency subscription billing.
The source treats subscription potential as a positive attribute, not a pass/fail criterion.

cards.title: Screen size, weight and shipping cost before you commit
cards.summary: Oversized or heavy products create shipping costs that deter buyers or eat margin, so estimate carrier costs on rough dimensions early.
cards.use_when: You are comparing product concepts and shipping economics matter to your margin.
steps: Measure or estimate the packed size and weight of the product as it would ship, not just the raw item.
Go to your carrier's website and price a rough shipment using those numbers to get a feel for real cost before sourcing.
Compare the result against your markup. If shipping consumes a large share of the spread between cost and price, the product needs a higher price point or a smaller format.
Prefer small and light formats. In the source example the hair mask was classified by most shippers as a small package in both weight and size, which kept shipping manageable.
Recheck shipping assumptions for the destinations your customer profile points to, since cross-border rates differ.
caveats: Carrier pricing and dimensional rules change over time; verify current rates before building them into a cost model.
Shipping cost estimates do not include inbound freight, packaging materials or returns.

cards.title: Design for durability to cut returns, breakage and refunds
cards.summary: Durability covers both packaging and product formulation, and directly reduces returns and in-transit damage.
cards.use_when: You are choosing materials, packaging or formulation for a shippable physical product.
steps: Assess the failure mode that would generate a return or refund, then design against it.
Choose packaging that survives parcel handling. The source's example prefers a plastic container over glass because it is cheaper and more reliable in transit.
Verify the product itself will not degrade, leak or separate during shipping and storage.
Consider ingredient or component quality as part of durability: the source argues for effective, safe ingredients so the product also holds up on performance, not just in transit.
Think about durability holistically across packaging and product; both drive returns and reviews.
caveats: Cheaper durable packaging can conflict with premium positioning; the source frames plastic as a practical margin decision, not a universal aesthetic rule.
Regulated categories may constrain packaging material choices.

cards.title: Map seasonality to protect cash flow
cards.summary: Identifying seasonal demand swings with Google Trends lets you plan inventory buys and marketing calendar around cash flow.
cards.use_when: You are validating a product whose demand may cluster in specific months, or planning inventory and ad budgets.
steps: Plot the core keywords in Google Trends across multiple years, looking for recurring monthly spikes.
Label the pattern: extreme seasonality (the source uses Christmas trees, almost all bought in November and December), mild seasonality, or year-round demand.
If seasonality exists, plan cash flow around it: inventory must be paid for before the spike, and off-season months still carry storage and overhead.
Use the seasonal pattern in marketing too. In the source example subtle January search spikes were interpreted as cold-weather hair rescue demand and noted for winter marketing.
Do not confuse mild seasonal variation with a fad; check whether the spikes repeat each year before treating them as predictable.
caveats: A mildly seasonal product can still be a strong business; the source keeps the data for campaign timing rather than rejecting the product.
Strong seasonality concentrates both revenue and risk, and complicates launching a new brand from zero.

cards.title: Prioritize products that solve a pain or serve a passion
cards.summary: Products tied to a real problem or an active hobby make customer acquisition easier than nice-to-have items.
cards.use_when: You are ranking several viable product ideas and want a qualitative tiebreaker on marketability.
steps: Classify each idea as solving a pain point, serving a passion, or merely nice to have.
Deprioritize nice-to-have products, which the source says are tougher to sell because the buyer has no urgency or identity stake.
Note that a product can do both. In the source example the hair mask treats dry or brittle hair (pain) while also serving people invested in keeping their hair healthy (passion).
Use the classification to shape positioning: pain-led products sell relief and outcomes, passion-led products sell identity, community and enthusiasm.
Combine with consumability (see the repeat-purchase card) because pain or passion plus repeat use compounds acquisition efficiency.
caveats: This is a qualitative judgement, not a measured threshold; the source treats it as one input among sixteen.
A pain-solving product in a crowded category can still fail on price and differentiation.

cards.title: Favor consumable and disposable formats for repeat business
cards.summary: Consumable products naturally generate repeat purchase and open the door to subscriptions and better lifetime value.
cards.use_when: Choosing between otherwise comparable product ideas, or building a retention plan.
steps: Prefer products the customer must rebuy: food, cleaning products and personal care such as the source's hair mask example.
Treat repeat purchase as a business advantage that improves the economics of acquiring a customer once.
Pair consumability with an honest replenishment cadence so repeat orders actually happen (see the subscription card).
Where the product is not inherently consumable, look for recurring add-ons, refills or accessories to create a repeat path.
Combine consumability with pain/passion positioning for the strongest retention profile.
caveats: Consumability does not guarantee repeat purchase: a bad first experience kills the second order.
Slow-consumption consumables produce weaker repeat frequency than daily-use products.

cards.title: Check shelf life and perishability before stocking inventory
cards.summary: Perishable goods risk dead stock and write-offs if sales are slow, so verify shelf life against your realistic sell-through window.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating food, cosmetics or any product with an expiry or degradation risk.
steps: Establish the product's shelf life in the condition it will be stored and shipped.

Compare that window against the time you need to build a marketing plan, generate sales and get the product in front of buyers. The source's example product had a shelf life of roughly three years or more, which it judged more than enough runway.
Also account for how long the customer takes to consume the product once delivered; a long customer-use window reduces pressure on the next order cycle.
If shelf life is short, plan smaller inventory buys and faster turns, and expect higher storage and waste cost.
Reject or redesign any perishable concept whose sell-through window is shorter than your realistic launch and ramp timeline.
caveats: The three-year shelf life is a case-study figure for coconut oil, not a general requirement.
Perishability risk rises sharply if your forecasts are optimistic or if shipping delays extend transit time.

cards.title: Research regulations and restrictions before investing in a category
cards.summary: Food, cosmetics, baby products and similar categories carry compliance requirements that should be identified before you spend on sourcing.
cards.use_when: Your product idea touches regulated categories or you are unsure whether claims, labelling or testing rules apply.
steps: Identify which regime your product falls into. The source names food, cosmetics and baby toys as categories that clearly require upfront research.
Check requirements for every country you plan to sell in, since labelling and ingredient rules differ by market.
Find out what the rules mean for your marketing claims, packaging copy and any testing or documentation obligations.
Do the research before investment, not after, because discovering a compliance blocker late wastes both time and money.
Record any restrictions as explicit concerns in your validation summary so the go/no-go decision accounts for them.
caveats: The source's example product had few restrictions, which is category-specific and not a general finding.
This card flags the need for research; it does not substitute for qualified regulatory or legal advice.

cards.title: Close validation with a written highlights-and-concerns summary
cards.summary: End the framework by stating what is working and what is not, so the decision to proceed is explicit rather than assumed.
cards.use_when: You have completed the sixteen validation questions and need to make a go/no-go call or justify one to a partner.
steps: List the highlights. In the source example they were low cost to start, strong search demand, a positive trend trajectory and rankable keywords.
List the concerns. The same example flagged the low price point and the competitive landscape.

Decide whether each concern can be answered by something under your control. The source says much of the potential success comes from building a strong brand around the product and from making the product more effective than the raw commodity alternative, such as plain coconut oil.
If concerns depend on market forces changing, treat the idea as a weaker bet than one whose concerns are fixable through branding, formulation or positioning.
Proceed when the concerns have a plausible plan, and revisit the summary after launch to check which assumptions held.
caveats: The source does not provide a scoring formula; it deliberately accepts unresolved red flags and relies on the operator's judgement.
A strong brand plan does not fix fundamentally thin unit economics in paid acquisition.

In the source example the hair mask was classified by most shippers as a small package in both weight and size, which kept shipping manageable.", "Recheck shipping assumptions for the destinations your customer profile points to, since cross-border rates differ."], "caveats": ["Carrier pricing and dimensional rules change over time; verify current rates before building them into a cost model.", "Shipping cost estimates do not include inbound freight, packaging materials or returns."], "tags": ["product-research", "logistics", "shipping-cost", "unit-economics", "product-validation"]}, {"title": "Design for durability to cut returns, breakage and refunds", "summary": "Durability covers both packaging and product formulation, and directly reduces returns and in-transit damage.", "use_when": "You are choosing materials, packaging or formulation for a shippable physical product.", "steps": ["Assess the failure mode that would generate a return or refund, then design against it.", "Choose packaging that survives parcel handling. The source's example prefers a plastic container over glass because it is cheaper and more reliable in transit.", "Verify the product itself will not degrade, leak or separate during shipping and storage.", "Consider ingredient or component quality as part of durability: the source argues for effective, safe ingredients so the product also holds up on performance, not just in transit.", "Think about durability holistically across packaging and product; both drive returns and reviews."], "caveats": ["Cheaper durable packaging can conflict with premium positioning; the source frames plastic as a practical margin decision, not a universal aesthetic rule.", "Regulated categories may constrain packaging material choices."], "tags": ["product-research", "logistics", "packaging", "returns", "product-validation"]}, {"title": "Map seasonality to protect cash flow", "summary": "Identifying seasonal demand swings with Google Trends lets you plan inventory buys and marketing calendar around cash flow.", "use_when": "You are validating a product whose demand may cluster in specific months, or planning inventory and ad budgets.", "steps": ["Plot the core keywords in Google Trends across multiple years, looking for recurring monthly spikes.", "Label the pattern: extreme seasonality (the source uses Christmas trees, almost all bought in November and December), mild seasonality, or year-round demand.", "If seasonality exists, plan cash flow around it: inventory must be paid for before the spike, and off-season months still carry storage and overhead.", "Use the seasonal pattern in marketing too. In the source example subtle January search spikes were interpreted as cold-weather hair rescue demand and noted for winter marketing.", "Do not confuse mild seasonal variation with a fad; check whether the spikes repeat each year before treating them as predictable."], "caveats": ["A mildly seasonal product can still be a strong business; the source keeps the data for campaign timing rather than rejecting the product.", "Strong seasonality concentrates both revenue and risk, and complicates launching a new brand from zero."], "tags": ["product-research", "seasonality", "cash-flow", "google-trends", "inventory-planning"]}, {"title": "Prioritize products that solve a pain or serve a passion", "summary": "Products tied to a real problem or an active hobby make customer acquisition easier than nice-to-have items.", "use_when": "You are ranking several viable product ideas and want a qualitative tiebreaker on marketability.", "steps": ["Classify each idea as solving a pain point, serving a passion, or merely nice to have.", "Deprioritize nice-to-have products, which the source says are tougher to sell because the buyer has no urgency or identity stake.", "Note that a product can do both. In the source example the hair mask treats dry or brittle hair (pain) while also serving people invested in keeping their hair healthy (passion).", "Use the classification to shape positioning: pain-led products sell relief and outcomes, passion-led products sell identity, community and enthusiasm.", "Combine with consumability (see the repeat-purchase card) because pain or passion plus repeat use compounds acquisition efficiency."], "caveats": ["This is a qualitative judgement, not a measured threshold; the source treats it as one input among sixteen.", "A pain-solving product in a crowded category can still fail on price and differentiation."], "tags": ["product-research", "product-validation", "positioning", "customer-research", "creative-strategy"]}, {"title": "Favor consumable and disposable formats for repeat business", "summary": "Consumable products naturally generate repeat purchase and open the door to subscriptions and better lifetime value.", "use_when": "Choosing between otherwise comparable product ideas, or building a retention plan.", "steps": ["Prefer products the customer must rebuy: food, cleaning products and personal care such as the source's hair mask example.", "Treat repeat purchase as a business advantage that improves the economics of acquiring a customer once.", "Pair consumability with an honest replenishment cadence so repeat orders actually happen (see the subscription card).", "Where the product is not inherently consumable, look for recurring add-ons, refills or accessories to create a repeat path.", "Combine consumability with pain/passion positioning for the strongest retention profile."], "caveats": ["Consumability does not guarantee repeat purchase: a bad first experience kills the second order.", "Slow-consumption consumables produce weaker repeat frequency than daily-use products."], "tags": ["product-research", "retention", "consumables", "ltv", "subscription", "product-validation"]}, {"title": "Check shelf life and perishability before stocking inventory", "summary": "Perishable goods risk dead stock and write-offs if sales are slow, so verify shelf life against your realistic sell-through window.", "use_when": "You are evaluating food, cosmetics or any product with an expiry or degradation risk.", "steps": ["Establish the product's shelf life in the condition it will be stored and shipped.", "Compare that window against the time you need to build a marketing plan, generate sales and get the product in front of buyers. The same example flagged the low price point and the competitive landscape.", "Decide whether each concern can be answered by something under your control. The source says much of the potential success comes from building a strong brand around the product and from making the product more effective than the raw commodity alternative, such as plain coconut oil.", "If concerns depend on market forces changing, treat the idea as a weaker bet than one whose concerns are fixable through branding, formulation or positioning.", "Proceed when the concerns have a plausible plan, and revisit the summary after launch to check which assumptions held."], "caveats": ["The source does not provide a scoring formula; it deliberately accepts unresolved red flags and relies on the operator's judgement.", "A strong brand plan does not fix fundamentally thin unit economics in paid acquisition."], "tags": ["product-research", "product-validation", "go-no-go", "positioning", "decision-making"]}]}

input.text:
02-PRD / Product Validation Framework

Goes here. Baseline qualitative and quantitative frameworks for validating new e-commerce physical product ideas prior to manufacturing or sourcing. Covers market demand analysis, unit economics estimates, logistical constraints (weight, durability, perishability), and demographic validation criteria.

Not here. • Active product scouting via ad spy tools or native ad scraping -> [02-PRD] / Direct Response Product Scouting • Supplier negotiation, purchasing inventory, and physical manufacturing -> [06-OPS] / Supply Chain & Sourcing • Setting up the actual e-commerce storefront or landing page -> [05-WEB] / Storefront Architecture

Header. url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KMrTD8KIB18 source_date: 2021-07 verified_at: 2026-09-19 rights: public_reference why: A comprehensive 16-point baseline checklist for validating e-commerce physical products spanning market demand, logistics, unit economics, and customer intent. modules: [[02-PRD]] topics: [[Product Validation, Market Sizing, Unit Economics, SKU Management, Logistics Constraints, Trend Analysis]] tier: 1 scope_hint: baseline decay_risk: low

Topics. • Market Demand & Trend Analysis

Sizing search volume and social mentions.

Differentiating between passing fads and growing macro trends.

Analyzing seasonality swings (e.g., winter spikes) for cash flow mapping. • Competitive Analysis & Local Availability

Fragmented markets vs. monopoly leaders.

Offline scarcity (if it is easily bought at a local grocery store, online viability drops). • Unit Economics & Pricing Strategy

Target retail price sweet spots for paid acquisition.

Margin and markup safety nets. • Logistics & Physical Constraints

SKU count management and inventory complexity.

Shipping constraints (size, weight, durability).

Shelf-life and perishability risks. • Customer Retention & Friction

Solving a pain vs. serving a passion.

Consumability and subscription (CPA/LTV) potential.

Look for. • Demand validation mechanics: Use Google Keyword Planner for monthly search volume and BuzzSumo for daily social media mentions. • Trend validation mechanics: Cross-reference keywords in Google Trends to identify upward trajectories and seasonal purchasing behaviors. • Pricing threshold: Target a $50 to $150 retail price sweet spot. This allows sufficient markup to absorb paid advertising costs (CAC) while staying low enough to avoid expectations of premium phone support. • SKU mechanics: Launch with exactly 1 SKU to minimize initial inventory capital, storage costs, and shipping mix-ups. • Logistics criteria: Select products that are small, lightweight, highly durable (e.g., plastic packaging instead of glass to reduce breakage), and non-perishable (e.g., 3+ year shelf life) to protect profit margins from shipping overhead and dead stock. • Retention mechanics: Prioritize consumable or disposable products (e.g., supplements, cosmetics) to naturally generate repeat business and enable subscription models.

Skip. Do not capture promotional mentions of the Shopify 14-day free trial or links to their free 40-minute webinar. Exclude generic YouTube intro/outro dialogue (e.g., "hit the subscribe button").

Scope mix. 100% baseline (fundamental product evaluation criteria that do not change over time).

Volume. ~250 words.
